title: Enoch's farewell and the end of the Ten Weeks
sum: Enoch calls Methuselah and all his family together. A spirit has come on him, and he wants to show them what will happen "forever." He tells them to love uprightness, to avoid a double heart, and to walk in the paths of righteousness, because violence will grow, the Flood will come, injustice will grow again, and God will judge the earth a second time. The righteous will rise from their sleep (91:10).

In the middle of the chapter (91:11–17) stand the last three of the "Ten Weeks" of world history: the eighth week of the righteous sword and a house for the Great King, the ninth when judgment is revealed to the whole world, and the tenth when the Watchers are judged and a new heaven appears. These verses belong after 93:10. The Aramaic scroll 4Q212 from Qumran shows the original order, and something went wrong in the copying before the Ethiopic was made. The site keeps the usual verse numbers, so read 93:1–10 first and then come back to 91:11.
readings: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads the chapter as Enoch's own farewell, a true prophecy of the Flood, of the last judgment and of the new creation, given to his family and handed down.
Read as a Jewish writing of the 100s BC

Most scholars see an introduction written for the Epistle. The writer uses Enoch's authority to speak to his own community in Judea, telling them that the violence they suffer will end and that they belong to God's plan.

views.E: A true prophecy of Enoch, read in the Ethiopian Church as part of the Old Testament. Its two judgments are the Flood and the last judgment, and its new heaven is the one Christ will bring.
views.H: An introduction to the Epistle (91:1–10, 18–19) wrapped around the end of the Apocalypse of Weeks (91:11–17), which was moved here in the copying. Probably written in Judea in the 100s BC.
views.N: The chapter's two ways (91:18–19), the Flood as a pattern of the end (91:5–7), the resurrection of the righteous (91:10) and the new heaven (91:16) are all ideas the New Testament shares (Matthew 7:13–14; Matthew 24:37–39; 2 Peter 3:5–13; Revelation 21:1).
views.J: Copied at Qumran (4Q212). Its call to walk in uprightness with an undivided heart sounds like later Jewish ethics; the rabbis did not use the book but taught the same two inclinations and the two paths.
views.W: Worth reading as a witness to Jewish hope before Christ. The picture of the end agrees with the Bible in outline; its schedule of weeks is not Scripture for most churches.

deep.h: How the Ten Weeks got out of order
deep.b:
The "Apocalypse of Weeks" divides all history into ten weeks. In every Ethiopic manuscript, weeks one to seven are in 93:3–10, and weeks eight to ten are earlier, in 91:12–17. R. H. Charles already suspected that the page had been misplaced, and in 1976 J. T. Milik published the Aramaic fragments of 4Q212 (4QEnoch-g), a scroll copied in the first century BC. In its fourth column the end of the seventh week (93:9–10) is followed directly by the text of 91:11–17.

So the original order was 93:1–10, then 91:11–17. Scholars think a scribe, or the Greek translator, put a block of text in the wrong place. Several modern translations (Charles, Nickelsburg–VanderKam) print the passage in the Aramaic order; others keep the Ethiopic order. This site keeps Charles's verse numbers, which scholars use for citing 1 Enoch, and explains the order in notes.

Dillmann's Ge'ez is cut into verses for this site by machine, following the Ethiopian Church's printed text. At a few edges the cut still falls a word or two off: the word "sevenfold" that ends 91:16 sits at the start of 91:17. The Plain follows the sense.

deep.title: Claude's theory: why the weeks moved
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. The Ethiopic order may not be a pure accident. Someone who read 91:5–10 (violence grows, punishment comes, the righteous rise) might have felt that 91:11–17 (roots of injustice cut off, the righteous judge, a new heaven) belonged right there as its fulfillment, and moved it. If so, the change was an early act of interpretation, joining Enoch's farewell to the end of history. Published scholars usually explain the move as a mechanical slip in copying; I have not seen this suggestion in print, and the evidence for either is thin.

echoes: Genesis 6:11–13; Deuteronomy 30:15–19; Psalm 1:6; Isaiah 30:26; Isaiah 65:17; Daniel 12:2; Matthew 7:13–14; 2 Peter 3:5–13; Revelation 21:1

settings.by: Enoch, with a spirit poured out on him
settings.to: Methuselah, his brothers and all Enoch's relatives, gathered at his call
settings.when: before Enoch leaves the earth, in the story's time before the Flood
settings.why: To pass on what he has learned: love uprightness, refuse a double heart, and know that God will judge violence twice, in the Flood and at the end.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.what: The Apocalypse of Weeks, weeks eight to ten
settings.by: Enoch, reading from the heavenly books
settings.why: To show that after the bad seventh week, history will turn: the righteous will judge, a house will be built for the Great King, the world will be judged, and a new heaven will come.
settings.readers: Jewish scribes in Judea, probably shortly before the Maccabean revolt (about 170 BC), who saw their own small group as the chosen ones of the seventh week.
views: Before the Maccabean revolt
Most scholars date the Apocalypse of Weeks before 167 BC, since it says nothing of Antiochus IV's persecution.
During the revolt
Some read the sword of 91:12 as the Maccabean war, and date it to the 160s BC.

settings.why: To make the choice plain: walk in the paths of righteousness, not of violence, because the second path ends in ruin.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

title: The opening of Enoch's letter
sum: This short chapter is the heading of the "Epistle of Enoch": Enoch the scribe wrote this complete teaching of wisdom for his children and for the generations to come who will practice uprightness and peace. Then comes a word of comfort: do not grieve over the times, for the Holy Great One has set days for everything.

The righteous one will rise from sleep and walk in goodness and in eternal light, while sin perishes in darkness forever. The Greek papyrus that preserves the end of these chapters calls the whole work an Epistle (a letter), and many scholars think it once began here.

views.E: Enoch's letter to all his spiritual children, which the Ethiopian Church still reads. "The generations to come" include the church.
views.H: The superscription of the Epistle, probably once the start of a separate book (92:1–105:2) before chapter 91 was added in front.
views.N: The resurrection to light and the comfort that God has set the times are close to Paul's words to the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 4:13–5:5) and Acts 1:7.
views.J: The Aramaic 4Q212 includes this part, with different titles for Enoch ("the scribe of distinction," as Milik restores it). "Enoch the scribe" fits the Second Temple image of Enoch as the first writer and sage.
views.W: A helpful window into how Jews read their times as part of God's calendar. It adds no doctrine the Bible lacks.

echoes: Genesis 18:25; Ecclesiastes 3:1; Daniel 12:2; Acts 1:7; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–5:5; 1 John 1:5–7

settings.what: The heading and opening comfort of the Epistle
settings.to: "all my children who live on the earth" and the generations to come
settings.when: written down as a letter for later readers
settings.why: To present what follows as Enoch's complete wisdom and to steady readers who are troubled "because of the times": the days are set, and the righteous will rise.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

title: Ten weeks of history
sum: Enoch reads from the books what he learned in his vision, from the angels and from the heavenly tablets. History is ten "weeks." He was born seventh in the first week. In the second week evil grows, the first end (the Flood) comes and one man (Noah) is saved. In the third a man (Abraham) is chosen as the plant of righteousness; in the fourth come visions and a law for all generations (Moses and Sinai); in the fifth the house of glory and the kingdom (Solomon's temple). In the sixth people go blind, a man goes up (Elijah), the house is burned and the chosen root is scattered (the exile). The seventh is a perverse generation, but at its end chosen righteous ones receive sevenfold wisdom.

The story continues in 91:11–17 (weeks eight to ten). Then 93:11–14 asks: who can hear God's voice, measure the earth or count the stars? No human can, unless God shows him, and the reader knows that God showed Enoch.
readings: As a summary of the Bible's story
Each week packs a book of the Hebrew Bible into one line. Reading the weeks with Genesis, Exodus and Kings side by side shows what the writer valued: covenant, law, temple, and a chosen remnant.
As the writer's own place in history
The weeks run fast to the seventh, where the writer stands. The point is that his small group is the climax of the story, the chosen plant at the end of a crooked age.

views.E: A true prophecy given before the Flood. Ethiopian teachers read the later weeks as reaching to Christ and the church, the chosen from the eternal plant.
views.H: An "apocalypse" written shortly before the Maccabean revolt (about 170 BC). It reviews Israel's history as a riddle and places the writer's group at the turning point. Its silence about the rebuilt temple is a criticism of the temple of the writer's day.
views.N: Dividing history into periods appears in Daniel 9, in Matthew's three sets of fourteen generations (Matthew 1:17) and in Paul's "fullness of time" (Galatians 4:4). Jude 14 calls Enoch "the seventh from Adam," as 93:3 does.
views.J: The Aramaic 4Q212 preserves much of it. Its idea of a chosen "plant" is shared by the Dead Sea Scrolls (Damascus Document 1:7). Later rabbinic chronology also divides history into ages, but not with these weeks.
views.W: A remarkable Jewish reading of the Old Testament's story. Its claim to be predicted by Enoch is accepted as Scripture only in the Ethiopian churches; other readers value it as history of interpretation.

deep.b:
WeekWhat the text saysWhat most readers see
1 (93:3)Enoch born seventh; justice still holdsAdam to Enoch (Genesis 5)
2 (93:4)Great evil; the first end; a man saved; a law for sinnersThe Watchers, the Flood, Noah, Genesis 9
3 (93:5)A man chosen as the plant of righteous judgmentAbraham
4 (93:6)Visions; a law for all generations; an enclosureMoses, Sinai, the tabernacle
5 (93:7)The house of glory and kingdom builtSolomon's temple
6 (93:8)Blindness; a man goes up; the house burned; the root scatteredThe kings, Elijah, 586 BC, exile

9 (91:14)Judgment revealed to the whole worldJudgment of the nations

deep.title: Claude's theory: the questions have an answer
deep.b: This is my own reading, though it overlaps with Nickelsburg and Stuckenbruck, who also connect 93:11–14 with Enoch's journeys. The questions of 93:11–14 sound like God's questions to Job, which expect the answer "no one." But in the Enoch library the answer is "Enoch": he heard the Holy One's voice (14:24), saw the ends of the earth and heaven (chapters 17–36), and learned the number and paths of the stars (chapters 72–82). Placed right after the Ten Weeks, the questions may be a quiet claim that the history just told comes from the only human who has seen these things, and so cannot be checked by ordinary wisdom.

echoes: Genesis 5:3–24; Genesis 6–9; Genesis 12:1–3; Exodus 19–24; 1 Kings 6–8; 2 Kings 2:11; 2 Kings 25:9; Daniel 9:24–27; Job 38:4–33; Isaiah 40:12; Jude 14

settings.what: The Apocalypse of Weeks, weeks one to seven
settings.by: Enoch, reading from the heavenly books
settings.why: To show his children the whole plan of history, so that later readers in the seventh week would know they are the chosen plant and that the turn of history is near.
settings.readers: Jewish scribes in Judea, probably shortly before the Maccabean revolt (about 170 BC), who saw their own small group as the chosen ones of the seventh week.

settings.what: Questions about what no human can know
settings.why: To set revealed knowledge apart from human cleverness: no one can know heaven and earth unless God shows him.
settings.readers: The same Judean scribal circle, who prized Enoch's revealed knowledge of heaven and earth above other wisdom.

title: Two paths and the first woes
sum: Enoch urges his children to love righteousness, keep far from the paths of violence and death, and choose "a life worth choosing." He warns that sinners will tempt people to abuse wisdom.

Then the woes begin: woe to those who build injustice, who build their houses with sin, who pile up gold and silver; woe to the rich who trust in their wealth and forgot the Most High. They are ready for the day of slaughter, and their Creator will rejoice at their fall. These cries of "woe" will fill the next six chapters.

views.E: The Ethiopian Church hears these woes as moral teaching for all times: against greed, injustice and forgetting God in prosperity.
views.H: The woes speak to a real conflict in Judea in the 100s BC between powerful landowners and a group of poor, devout Jews. The writer's community uses Enoch's voice to condemn its oppressors.
views.N: Jesus' woes on the rich in Luke 6:24–26, the parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16–21) and James 5:1–6 are very close in tone and ideas.
views.J: The prophetic woe (Isaiah 5; Amos 6; Habakkuk 2) is reused here in a new way. The rabbis did not keep this book, but similar warnings about wealth fill the Mishnah's Avot.
views.W: A strong ancient sermon on social justice in line with the prophets and Jesus. Its harsh joy at the sinners' fall is to be read alongside God's wish that the wicked repent (Ezekiel 18:23).

deep.h: Who were the rich and the righteous?
deep.b:
The woes never name a ruler or a city, but they paint a clear picture. The "sinners" are rich: they build houses with forced labor (99:13), own estates with many workers (97:9), wear purple (98:2), eat the best wheat (96:5), lend and curse and bribe (95:4; 100:12), and control the courts (103:14–15). They twist the law and the words of uprightness (99:2; 104:10). The "righteous" are poor, powerless and persecuted (103:9–15), with no court to hear them.

Most scholars place this in Judea in the 100s BC, when Greek-style wealth and power grew among Jewish elites, whether before the Maccabean revolt or under the Hasmonean kings around 100 BC. George Nickelsburg showed how close these chapters are to the Gospel of Luke's teaching on wealth. The first hearers were real people in real distress, and the woes were meant to give them courage: the rich will not have the last word.

echoes: Deuteronomy 8:11–14; Deuteronomy 30:19; Isaiah 5:8–23; Jeremiah 22:13; Amos 6:1; Habakkuk 2:9–12; Luke 6:24–26; Luke 12:16–21; James 5:1–6

settings.when: opening the main body of the Epistle
settings.why: To urge the faithful to keep to the path of righteousness and to keep Enoch's words in their hearts when sinners tempt them.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.to: spoken against the rich and unjust, for the ears of the righteous
settings.when: the first of about thirty woes in chapters 94–100
settings.why: To announce the sudden ruin of those who build with injustice and trust in wealth, so the oppressed will not envy or fear them.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.
views: Hellenizing elites
Many date the Epistle before the Maccabean revolt and see the rich as aristocrats who embraced Greek ways.
Hasmonean rulers
Others date it around 100 BC and see the rich as the ruling class under the Hasmonean kings.

title: Enoch weeps
sum: Enoch wishes his eyes were a rain cloud so he could weep over the sinners. Then he tells the righteous not to fear them: the Lord will again hand the sinners over to them.

Four woes follow: against those who lay curses that cannot be lifted, who repay their neighbors with evil, who give false testimony and weigh out injustice, and who hunt down the righteous. Each will be paid back in kind.

views.E: Enoch weeps like Jeremiah over the lost. The Ethiopian Church reads the woes against curses and false witnesses as part of its moral teaching.
views.H: The woes describe abuses of law and religion (bans, false witnesses, rigged courts) by the powerful in the writer's society.
views.N: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41) and pronounces woes (Matthew 23). Paul warns against repaying evil for evil (Romans 12:17).
views.J: "Who will give me..." is a Hebrew idiom, a sign that the Ge'ez goes back through Greek to a Semitic original.
views.W: A moving picture of a prophet's grief and of justice that mirrors the crime. It agrees closely with the prophets.

echoes: Jeremiah 9:1; Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12; Obadiah 15; Matthew 16:19; Luke 19:41; Romans 2:6; Romans 12:17

settings.why: To show that the judge also mourns: the woes are not glee but grief over coming ruin.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.why: To free the righteous from fear and to name the crimes of their oppressors, each of which will turn back on its doer.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

title: Hope, you righteous
sum: The righteous are told to hope: the sinners will perish before them. On the day of the sinners' trouble the young of the righteous will soar like eagles and hide in the rocks like rock badgers, while the unjust groan and wail. Those who suffered will be healed and will hear a voice of rest from heaven.

Then come woes on the sinners whose wealth makes them look righteous, on those who eat the finest wheat and trample the lowly, who drink water at every hour but have left the spring of life, and on the mighty who crush the righteous.

views.E: A promise of comfort and rest for all who suffer for righteousness, read in the Ethiopian Church alongside Christ's beatitudes.
views.H: The contrast of luxury and hunger reflects real economic conditions; water and wheat were symbols of the rich land owner's power.
views.N: "Rest" from heaven (96:3) and the "spring of life" (96:6) are themes of Revelation 14:13, Revelation 21:6 and John 4:10–14.
views.J: The images of eagles, rock badgers and the spring of life all come from the Hebrew Bible (Psalm 104:18; Jeremiah 2:13).
views.W: Its denial that wealth proves righteousness agrees with Job, Psalm 73 and Jesus.

echoes: Psalm 104:18; Proverbs 30:26; Isaiah 40:31; Jeremiah 2:13; Amos 6:6; Revelation 14:13; John 4:10–14

settings.why: To give the oppressed hope of safety and healing when the sinners fall.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.what: Woes on the rich and mighty
settings.to: spoken against the rich, the luxurious and the mighty
settings.why: To unmask the rich, whose wealth looks like blessing, and to promise that the righteous will see better days.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

title: The prayer of the righteous and the boast of the rich
sum: The righteous are told to believe that the sinners will be put to shame. The Most High has the sinners' destruction in mind, and the angels will rejoice. What will the sinners do when they hear the prayer of the righteous? That prayer will reach the Lord, and every word of their injustice will be read out before the Holy Great One.

Then the rich speak for themselves: "We have become rich, truly rich... Now let us do what we have planned." Enoch answers that their wealth will run away like water. From 97:6 on, an older Greek copy of these chapters survives, the Chester Beatty–Michigan papyrus.

views.E: Prayer as the weapon of the weak: the Ethiopian Church reads it as teaching that God hears the cry of the oppressed.
views.H: The quoted boast gives a vivid picture of the estate-owning rich of the writer's day.
views.N: Close to Luke 12:16–21 (the rich fool) and Revelation 3:17 ("I am rich"). The prayers of the saints that bring judgment appear in Revelation 6:9–10 and 8:3–5.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition also tells of heaven's books and of prayers ascending, but did not preserve this book.
views.W: A powerful parallel to Jesus' teaching; read as a witness to Jewish thought, not as an added gospel.

deep.b:
For 97:6–107:3 we have more than the Ge'ez. A papyrus book of the 300s AD, part of which is in the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin and part at the University of Michigan, contains these chapters in Greek. Campbell Bonner published it in 1937 as The Last Chapters of Enoch in Greek. It has gaps, it lacks chapter 105, and it ends at 107:3 with the title "Epistle of Enoch." The Ethiopic was translated from a Greek text like this one.

The text in this site's sources is Dillmann's Ge'ez, so the Plain translates the Ge'ez. This part has not compared the Greek verse by verse. Where a Greek reading is given (for example "this letter" at 100:6), it is reported from Bonner's edition, and notes say where the Greek covers a verse that has not been checked.

echoes: Genesis 4:10; Exodus 3:7; Daniel 7:10; Proverbs 23:5; Luke 12:16–21; James 5:1–6; Revelation 3:17; Revelation 6:9–10

settings.why: To assure the faithful that their prayers reach God and that the sinners' words will be read out in the heavenly court.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.what: Woes on the rich, with their own boast
settings.to: the rich who gain wealth unjustly
settings.why: To let the rich condemn themselves by their own words, and to show how quickly unjust wealth disappears.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

title: Sin is made by people
sum: Enoch begins to swear oaths. The rich men dress in more finery than women, but they lack wisdom and will perish with their wealth. He swears that sin was not sent down on the earth: people created it themselves. Every sin is written down in heaven every day.

Woes follow on fools, on the stiff-hearted who eat blood, on lovers of injustice, on those who are glad when the righteous suffer, on those who brush aside the words of the righteous, and on those who write lying words.

views.E: The Ethiopian Church reads 98:4 alongside the Watchers story: evil spirits tempt, but every person is responsible for sin.
views.H: Many scholars see 98:4 as a deliberate correction of the Watchers myth (10:8), placing blame on human choice. The woes against writers of lies hint at quarrels over books and teaching.
views.N: James 1:13–15 says each person is tempted by his own desire. Romans 5:12 says sin entered through one man.
views.J: Later rabbis taught that the evil inclination is inside every person (the yetzer hara), close to 98:4, without the Watchers story.
views.W: 98:4 is close to the Bible's teaching of human responsibility. 98:5 uses barrenness as an example in that argument; as a rule about childless women it would conflict with the Bible's stories of Sarah, Rachel and Hannah.

echoes: Genesis 3:1–6; Genesis 9:4; Psalm 49:7–8; Psalm 94:7–9; Malachi 3:16; James 1:13–15; Romans 5:12; Revelation 20:12

settings.to: "both wise and foolish," then the sinners
settings.when: the first of a series of oaths in the Epistle
settings.why: To make his warnings as certain as a court verdict: wealth cannot save, sin is the sinners' own doing, and every deed is recorded.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.to: spoken against fools, the stiff-hearted, and writers of lies
settings.why: To warn that rejecting the words of the righteous and writing lies leads to sudden death.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

title: Woes on those who twist the law
sum: Woes fall on those who praise lies, twist the words of uprightness and break the eternal law. The righteous are told to lift their prayers as a witness before the angels. In those days nations will be shaken and the desperate will abandon even their nursing babies.

Enoch swears that sin is being made ready for a day of endless bloodshed. Idol-worshipers, who worship stones and demons, will find no help. In the middle stands a beatitude: blessed are those who accept wisdom and walk in righteousness, for they will be saved. Then more woes: on those who spread evil, build with others' labor, reject their fathers' inheritance and kill their neighbors.

views.E: The Ethiopian Church reads the warnings against idols and demons, and the beatitude of 99:10, as teaching for the faithful in every age.
views.H: The sinners are Jews who, in the writer's eyes, have left the ancestral law. The idolatry may be literal pagan cults or a charge against Hellenized Jews.
views.N: 99:7 closely matches Revelation 9:20; the intercession of angels matches Revelation 8:3–4 and Tobit 12:12.
views.J: "The eternal law" and "the inheritance of their fathers" show loyalty to the Torah and the land, central to Jewish identity.
views.W: Its teaching on idols and on blessing for the wise matches the Bible. Whether angels carry our prayers is a point where churches differ.

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:17; Psalm 106:37; Psalm 115:4–8; Isaiah 24:5; Jeremiah 22:13; Lamentations 4:3–10; Revelation 8:3–4; Revelation 9:20; 1 Corinthians 10:20

settings.to: spoken against those who twist uprightness
settings.why: To warn those who distort the law that they will be trampled.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.what: A call to prayer, signs of the end, and a beatitude
settings.when: in the middle of the woes
settings.why: To tell the righteous to bring their case to heaven in prayer, and to set the blessing of the wise against the fate of idolaters.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.why: To name the crimes of the powerful and promise that God's anger will throw down their glory.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

traditions.q: Do angels carry our prayers to God and pray for us?
views: Catholic
Yes. Angels watch over and intercede for people, and the faithful may ask their help (Catechism of the Catholic Church 334–336).
Orthodox
Yes. The angels pray for us, and the church asks for their prayers in its services, especially to the archangels Michael and Gabriel.
Ethiopian Orthodox

Yes. Angels such as Michael and Gabriel carry prayers and intercede, and the church keeps monthly days in their honor (Michael on the 12th, Gabriel on the 19th); passages like 1 Enoch 99:3 and Tobit 12:12 are read in this light.
Reformed
Angels serve God's people (Hebrews 1:14), but Christ is the only mediator (1 Timothy 2:5); worship and prayer are given to God alone, not to angels (Westminster Confession 21.2).
Baptist
Angels minister to believers, but prayers go directly to God through Christ, and no one should pray to or through angels (Colossians 2:18).

title: The day of slaughter and the witnesses of heaven
sum: In those days the sinners will kill one another, fathers with sons and brothers with brothers, until blood runs like a river and a horse wades in it up to its chest. Angels will gather all who helped sin, and the Most High will rise to judge. Over the righteous he will set holy angels as guards; even if they sleep a long sleep, they have nothing to fear. Then the wise will understand "this book."

Woes follow on those who torment and burn the righteous, who plot evil at night, and whose mouths and hands have sinned. Sun, moon, stars, clouds, dew and rain will testify against them. Enoch mocks them: try bribing the rain.

views.E: God's protection of the righteous by angels and his judgment of persecutors, read as true prophecy of the last day.
views.H: The violence imagined here answers the violence the community suffered (100:7). Burning the righteous may reflect real persecution or be a general picture.
views.N: The blood up to a horse's chest is close to Revelation 14:20; families turning on each other is in Mark 13:12; guardian angels in Matthew 18:10.
views.J: Later rabbinic texts use the image of blood rising to horses' nostrils for Rome's slaughter at Betar (AD 135), showing the image lived on.
views.W: The judgment scenes match Revelation's in outline. Readers are reminded that vengeance belongs to God (Romans 12:19).

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:10; Deuteronomy 11:17; Deuteronomy 30:19; Psalm 91:11; Micah 2:1; Micah 7:6; Mark 13:12; Matthew 18:10; Revelation 14:20

settings.what: An oracle of the last judgment
settings.when: in the middle of the woes
settings.why: To show the end of the sinners' power, the angels' protection of the righteous, and the vindication of Enoch's book.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.what: Woes, and creation as a witness
settings.why: To assure the persecuted that their sufferings are seen by all creation and will be judged.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

title: Look at the sea
sum: Enoch calls the hearers to look at heaven and fear God. If God shuts the windows of heaven, what will they do? Look at the ship captains: tossed by waves and winds, they fear the sea that may swallow them and all their goods.

But the sea itself is God's work. He sealed it in with sand, and at his rebuke it dries up. He made heaven and earth and gave wisdom to every living thing. The sailors fear the sea, yet sinners do not fear the Most High.

views.E: A wisdom lesson: creation teaches the fear of God. Ethiopian teachers read it with Psalm 104 and Job 38.
views.H: A wisdom poem using the argument from creation. The sailors and their cargo fit a commercial world the rich of Judea took part in.
views.N: Jesus calms the sea and the disciples ask who he is (Mark 4:39–41). Paul says creation shows God's power so that people are without excuse (Romans 1:20).
views.J: The picture of God setting the sea's boundary is from Jeremiah 5:22 and Job 38. Jonah's sailors fear the sea and then the LORD (Jonah 1:16).
views.W: Fully in line with the Bible's wisdom books: the creature should fear the Creator.

echoes: Job 38:8–11; Psalm 104:9; Psalm 107:23–30; Jeremiah 5:22; Jonah 1:4–16; Nahum 1:4; Mark 4:39–41; Romans 1:20

settings.what: A wisdom speech from the sea
settings.to: the sinners, addressed as "children of heaven"
settings.why: To shame the sinners with an example: sailors fear the sea, but sinners do not fear the God who made it.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

title: Do not fear death, you righteous
sum: When God brings fire and sends out his voice, the lights of heaven, the earth and even the angels will shake, and the sinners will be cursed forever.

Then Enoch turns to the souls of the righteous who have died. Do not grieve that you went down to Sheol in grief and got no reward in life. The sinners say, "The righteous die just as we die... from now on we are equal." They enjoy eating, drinking and robbing. But look at how the righteous ended: in peace. The chapter is one of the earliest Jewish answers to the question of why the good suffer and die unrewarded.

views.E: Comfort for the faithful dead, who live in God's care. The Ethiopian Church prays for the dead and honors the saints, and reads this passage in that light.
views.H: A debate with Jews who denied any judgment after death (compare Ecclesiastes 9:2). The writer insists that death is not the end.
views.N: Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 has a similar speech of the ungodly; the hope of the righteous dead matches Revelation 6:9–11 and 1 Corinthians 15:32.
views.J: Later the Sadducees denied resurrection (Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8). This passage shows the opposite view already strong among some Jews.
views.W: An important witness to belief in life after death before Christ, in harmony with Daniel 12 and the New Testament.

deep.b:
Chapters 102–104 are a debate. The sinners quote the hard facts: the righteous die just like everyone else, often in misery, and get nothing for their goodness. Their words sound like Ecclesiastes (Ecclesiastes 3:19–21; 9:2–3), a book the Bible itself includes. Enoch does not deny the facts. He denies that death is the end: the souls of the righteous live (103:3–4), their names are written in heaven (104:1), and they will shine like the stars (104:2).

Wisdom of Solomon 2:1–5:23 makes the same argument, perhaps a century later, and Paul quotes the sinners' creed, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" (1 Corinthians 15:32). For the first readers this was not theory. Members of their group had died poor and persecuted, and some may have been killed (100:7).

echoes: Psalm 29:3–9; Psalm 37:37; Ecclesiastes 3:19–21; Ecclesiastes 9:2–3; Isaiah 22:13; Wisdom of Solomon 2:1–5; 1 Corinthians 15:32; Revelation 6:9–11

settings.when: after the speech from the sea
settings.why: To picture God's terrible coming, when all creation shakes and only the sinners are cursed.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.what: Comfort for the righteous dead, answering the sinners
settings.to: "the souls of the righteous" who have died
settings.when: at the heart of the Epistle
settings.why: To answer the claim that death makes everyone equal: the righteous dead have a reward waiting for them.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment. Some of their members had died poor or been killed.

traditions.q: Are the souls of the righteous dead alive and aware before the resurrection?
views: Catholic

Yes. Each soul meets God in a particular judgment at death; the saved who need it are purified, and the blessed already see God before the resurrection of the body (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1021–1032).
Orthodox
Yes. The souls of the departed live and await the resurrection, already tasting joy or sorrow; the church prays for them.
Ethiopian Orthodox
Yes. The souls of the righteous rest with God and the saints pray for the living; the church prays for the dead, and texts like 1 Enoch 102:4–103:4 support this hope.
Reformed
Yes. At death the souls of believers are made perfect in holiness and go at once into glory, waiting for the resurrection (Westminster Shorter Catechism 37).
Adventist
No. The dead are unconscious, "asleep," until Christ returns and raises them (Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Beliefs 26).
Jehovah's Witnesses
No. The dead do not exist consciously; they wait in God's memory for a resurrection.

title: The righteous dead and the lament of the living
sum: Enoch swears by God's glory that he has read the mystery in the heavenly tablets: every good thing is prepared for the spirits of those who died in righteousness, and their share is greater than that of the living. Their spirits will rejoice. But the sinners who died rich and honored, praised by their friends, will go down into darkness, chains and flame.

Then Enoch quotes the lament of the living righteous: we worked ourselves out, became the tail instead of the head, were robbed and killed, and when we complained to the rulers no one listened; they helped our oppressors and hid our murders. It is one of the most vivid pictures of the first readers' real lives anywhere in Jewish writing of this time.

views.E: The Ethiopian Church hears the lament as the cry of the faithful poor in every age, and the oath as God's promise to them.
views.H: 103:9–15 gives a rare view from below: small farmers and laborers losing their land and lives while courts protect the powerful.
views.N: Compare Hebrews 11:35–38 and James 5:1–6; the reversal of fortunes is the theme of Luke 16:19–31.
views.J: The lament reuses the language of the Psalms (Psalm 44) and Deuteronomy's curses (Deuteronomy 28:13, 44), asking how the covenant promises can fail the faithful.
views.W: An honest lament and a hope beyond death that the Bible shares (Psalm 73; Daniel 12:2–3).

echoes: Deuteronomy 28:13; Deuteronomy 28:44; Psalm 44:9–26; Psalm 73:3–26; Ecclesiastes 4:1; Isaiah 59:14–15; Luke 16:19–31; Jude 6

settings.what: Woe on the sinners who died at ease
settings.why: To answer the praise given to the rich who died in comfort: their souls go down to judgment.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.by: the living righteous, quoted by Enoch
settings.to: Enoch's hearers, who are told not to say this about the righteous
settings.why: To give honest voice to the community's suffering before answering it; knowing the readers lived this changes it from theory to testimony.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.
views: Said about the righteous
The Ge'ez tells the hearers not to say this about the righteous; the words are still the righteous' own complaint.
Said by the righteous
Some modern translators take the line as addressed to the righteous themselves: "you righteous, do not say."

title: You will shine like the stars
sum: Enoch answers the lament. The angels remember the righteous before God, and their names are written in heaven. Before, they were shamed; now they will shine like the lights of heaven, and the doors of heaven will open. They should keep crying out for justice, keep hoping, and keep far from the sinners, for they will be companions of the army of heaven. Every sin of the sinners is written down; light and darkness see it all.

Then Enoch reveals two mysteries about his books. Sinners will change and twist his words and write books of their own. But when his words are written truthfully, "in their own languages," books will be given to the righteous and the wise, and they will believe and rejoice in them.

views.E: The Ethiopian Church sees 104:11–13 fulfilled in its own keeping of Enoch's books in Ge'ez, given to the faithful as Scripture.
views.H: A claim of authority for the Enoch books against rival writings in a time of argument over texts and teaching.
views.N: The righteous shining like stars (Daniel 12:3; Matthew 13:43), being like the angels (Mark 12:25), names written in heaven (Luke 10:20), and warnings against changing a book (Revelation 22:18–19).
views.J: The concern for faithful copying and translation is a strong Jewish value, seen in the care of scribes for the Torah.
views.W: The hope matches the Bible closely. The claim that Enoch's books are themselves given by God is what most churches do not accept.

echoes: Daniel 12:1–4; Matthew 13:43; Mark 12:25; Luke 10:20; Luke 18:1–8; Deuteronomy 4:2; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 22:18–19

settings.why: To turn the community's despair into hope: heaven remembers them, and their reward is to shine with the angels.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment.

settings.when: closing the main body of the Epistle
settings.why: To warn against twisting Enoch's words and to promise that his true books will reach the righteous and the wise.
settings.readers: A Jewish scribal circle in Judea in the 100s BC that treasured the Enoch books: probably poor or powerless people who felt cheated and persecuted by rich and powerful Jews, and who hoped for God's judgment. They had Enoch's books and argued with others over which writings to trust.

title: I and my son
sum: In two verses the Lord himself speaks: the righteous are to testify to the children of the earth about their wisdom, for they are guides for the whole earth. "I and my son will be united with them forever, in the paths of uprightness." Peace is promised to the children of uprightness.

This short chapter is not in the Greek papyrus, which goes straight from 104:13 to 106:1, but the Aramaic copy 4Q204 seems to have contained it, as J. T. Milik restored the fragment. Milik thought the words "I and my son" were a later Christian addition; Christian readers have heard in them the Father and the Son.

views.E: God the Father and his Son promise to dwell with the faithful. The Ethiopian Church reads this as a prophecy of Christ.
views.H: Present in the Aramaic 4Q204 as Milik restores it, so the chapter is probably old and its absence from the Greek a copying slip. Milik judged "I and my son" too long for the gap and called it a Christian gloss; others read "my son" as Jewish (the Messiah, as in 4 Ezra 7:28, or Israel).
views.N: Close to John 14:23, where the Father and the Son come to make their home with the one who loves Jesus.
views.J: "My son" for the king or Messiah comes from Psalm 2:7; Jewish texts such as 4 Ezra use it. The chapter was copied at Qumran (4Q204), but whether this phrase was in it is uncertain.
views.W: A striking phrase, but too uncertain in origin to build any teaching on.

settings.by: the Lord, in the first person
settings.to: the righteous, as guides to the children of the earth
settings.when: after Enoch's mysteries about the books
settings.why: To send the righteous out as teachers and to promise God's and his son's lasting presence with them.
settings.readers: Jewish readers of the Epistle, since the Aramaic 4Q204 appears to have had this chapter; the words "I and my son" may come from a later Christian hand.
views: Jewish origin
The chapter was in the Aramaic, and "my son" fits Jewish uses for the Messiah (4 Ezra 7:28) or for Israel (Exodus 4:22).
Christian gloss
Milik judged the gap in 4Q204 too short for "I and my son" and took the phrase as a Christian addition (1976, pp. 68, 222).

title: A child who shines like the sun
sum: Methuselah's son Lamech has a son whose body is white as snow and red as a rose, whose hair is white as wool and whose eyes light up the house like the sun. As soon as he is born he speaks with the Lord. Lamech is afraid the child is not his but an angel's, and sends Methuselah to Enoch at the ends of the earth.

Enoch explains: in the days of Jared, some from heaven sinned with women and fathered children of flesh. A Flood will come for a year. This child is truly Lamech's son and will be saved with his three sons. Name him Noah, for he will be a remnant. The same story is told in the Aramaic Genesis Apocryphon from Qumran, where Lamech's wife Bitenosh swears the child is his.
readings: It fills the silence of Genesis 5:28–29 with a marvelous birth, showing Noah as the righteous man chosen from the womb.
As a story about the Watchers
It retells the Watchers' sin from the side of a worried father: the fear that angels have mixed with humans reaches even Noah's family, and Enoch's word clears it.

views.E: A true account of Noah's birth and Enoch's prophecy, read in the Ethiopian Church as part of Scripture.
views.H: An older Noah tradition (perhaps from a lost "Book of Noah") attached to the Epistle. The Genesis Apocryphon (1Q20, copied in the late first century BC or early first century AD) tells a longer form of the same story.
views.N: The glory of the child recalls descriptions of heavenly figures (Daniel 7:9; Revelation 1:14). Jesus and Peter use Noah's days as a picture of the end (Matthew 24:37–39; 1 Peter 3:20).
views.J: The Genesis Apocryphon and fragments 4Q204 show the story at Qumran. The rabbis did not keep it, and later tradition read the sons of God in Genesis 6 as human rulers.
views.W: A charming legend that the Bible does not tell. Its view of Genesis 6:1–4 is held by some Christians and rejected by many.

deep.b:
The Genesis Apocryphon (1Q20), an Aramaic scroll found in Qumran Cave 1 in 1947, retells Genesis with many additions. Its columns 2–5 tell Noah's birth in Lamech's own voice. Lamech suspects that his wife Bitenosh conceived by one of the Watchers; she reminds him of their love and swears by the Great Holy One that the child is his. Lamech then sends Methuselah to Enoch, who explains.

1 Enoch 106–107 is shorter and told by Enoch. It does not name Lamech's wife or have her swear, but it shares the key points: the child's shining appearance, Lamech's fear, the journey to Enoch, the Watchers' sin in the days of Jared, and the name Noah. Scholars think both drew on an older Noah tradition. Joseph Fitzmyer's commentary on the scroll is the standard guide.

echoes: Genesis 5:28–29; Genesis 6:1–4; Genesis 6:9–10; Genesis 7:11–13; Daniel 7:9; Matthew 24:37–39; 1 Peter 3:20; 2 Peter 2:4–5; Jude 6

settings.by: Enoch, telling the story in the first person
settings.to: inside the story, Methuselah, who carries Enoch's answer to Lamech
settings.when: before the Flood, when Noah is born to Lamech
settings.why: Inside the story, to calm Lamech's fear and reveal the child's role: he is truly Lamech's son and the remnant who will survive the Flood. For readers, to show that God saves a righteous remnant through judgment.
settings.readers: Jewish readers of the 100s BC who knew the Watchers story and older Noah traditions, later retold at length in the Genesis Apocryphon; added to the Epistle to show the pattern of judgment and rescue.

title: The name of Noah
sum: Enoch reads on the heavenly tablets that generation after generation will do wrong until a generation of righteousness arises; then sin will pass away and every good thing will come to the earth. He sends Methuselah to tell Lamech that the child is truly his.
Methuselah returns and names the child Noah, "for he will bring joy to the earth after all the destruction." The Greek papyrus of the Epistle ends here, with the title "Epistle of Enoch."

views.E: The "generation of righteousness" is fulfilled in Christ and the faithful; Noah is a figure of Christ who saves through the waters.
views.H: The Noah story ends with the hope of the Epistle: sin will go on until the righteous generation of the writer's day.
views.N: 1 Peter 3:20–21 compares Noah's rescue through water to baptism; Hebrews 11:7 praises his faith.
views.J: The name is explained from Genesis 5:29. Jewish writings often saw Noah as the one righteous man of his age (Sirach 44:17).
views.W: A legend that ends with a hope the whole Bible shares: God will finally end sin.

title: Another book of Enoch
sum: A closing appendix calls itself "another book" that Enoch wrote for Methuselah and for those who keep the law in the last days. Wait until sin passes away: the sinners' names will be wiped from the holy books, and they will burn in a place of shapeless chaos where there is no earth. Enoch sees a deep cloud, a blazing fire and shining mountains swaying, and hears crying. An angel tells him it is where the spirits of sinners and of those who twist the prophets are thrown.

Heaven also records the humble who made their bodies suffer, loved God more than gold, and blessed God while being trampled. God says he will call the spirits of the good from the generation of light, transform those born in darkness, and seat each faithful one on a throne of honor. They will shine, and the sinners will see them and cry out. Chapter 108 is found only in Ge'ez.

views.E: The last word of the book of Enoch in the Ethiopian Bible: comfort for those who suffer for God and warning of fire for the wicked.
views.H: A late appendix, missing in the Greek and Aramaic, perhaps from the first century AD. Its praise of those who 'afflict their bodies' may come from an ascetic Jewish or early Christian circle.
views.N: Children of light, thrones for the faithful (Matthew 19:28; Revelation 3:21), names blotted out of the book (Revelation 3:5) and a place of fire and weeping (Matthew 13:42).
views.J: The "generation of light" and "those born in darkness" sound like the Dead Sea Scrolls' sons of light and sons of darkness.
views.W: Many of its hopes are the New Testament's, but as a late addition its witness is to later belief, not to the earliest Enoch tradition.

echoes: Genesis 1:2; Exodus 32:32–33; Psalm 69:28; Psalm 39:5; Matthew 13:42; Matthew 19:28; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 3:21; Revelation 20:4; Hebrews 11:35–38; 1 Thessalonians 5:5

settings.what: Another book of Enoch: exhortation and vision
settings.by: Enoch; an angel explains the vision (108:6–15), and God's own voice breaks in (108:10–12)
settings.to: Methuselah and "those who will come after him and keep the law in the last days"
settings.when: presented as a further writing of Enoch
settings.why: To encourage faithful people who suffer, and who live a hard life for God, to wait: the sinners will burn and the faithful will shine on thrones of honor.
settings.readers: A later Jewish (or possibly early Christian) group, probably in the first century AD, who honored people who denied themselves and suffered for their faith.
views: Jewish
Most scholars think the chapter is Jewish, from about the first century BC or AD.
Christian
Some suggest a Christian hand, because of its ideals of self-denial and the light-and-darkness language.

traditions.q: Is the punishment of the wicked everlasting conscious torment?
views: Catholic
Yes. Hell is eternal separation from God; its chief pain is the loss of God (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1033–1035).
Orthodox
Yes, it is everlasting; many Orthodox teachers describe it as the experience of God's love by those who refuse it.
Ethiopian Orthodox
Yes. The church teaches eternal punishment for the unrepentant and reads 1 Enoch's places of fire with the Gospels' warnings.
Evangelical
Most hold everlasting conscious punishment; a significant minority, including John Stott, have argued that the lost are finally destroyed.
Adventist
No. The wicked are destroyed in the final fire and cease to exist; the fire is eternal in its result, not in its torment (Fundamental Beliefs 27).
Jehovah's Witnesses
No. The wicked are destroyed forever; there is no place of conscious torment.
